---
title: Pretraining and fine-tuning
description: "Learn from unlabeled histories by reconstructing hidden values, then adapt the model to a labeled outcome."
engine: markdown
---

Suppose you have many account histories but only a smaller collection with
settled dispute labels. Use the profile and transaction records from the
[event-history example](profile-context-and-a-second-outcome.qmd), with one
account snapshot per row. For now, leave out future outcomes and the extra
line-item and withdrawal context introduced in the
[account example](nested-context-and-account-outcomes.qmd).

Give those histories a learning role by hiding selected amounts or merchants
and recovering them from the remaining context. Then use labeled payments to
adapt the learned context to the operational outcome.

Pretraining uses a reconstruction task on a broad collection of records.
Fine-tuning starts from those learned weights and adapts the model to a specific
task. In relflow, both use `model.fit(...)`; the data and reconstruction
objectives determine what the model learns.

The foundation-model workflow is broad pretraining followed by adaptation to
downstream tasks, following [Stanford's description](https://crfm.stanford.edu/report.html).
For your own structured data, this means learning from histories, adapting
the trained schema to new objectives, and evaluating the resulting predictions
or reused representations. A newly constructed model starts untrained.
Establishing useful reuse across tasks requires held-out evaluation on those
tasks.

| Stage | Data | Objectives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Self-supervised pretraining | Records without task labels | Reconstruct sampled observed values with `rf.Mask(rate=..., reconstruct=True)`. |
| Supervised fine-tuning | Labeled task records | Predict always-hidden transaction labels with `mask=True`, optionally retaining reconstruction objectives. |
| Resume a run | The same training task | Restore the model, optimizer, scheduler, and loop progress from a full Lightning checkpoint. |

```{typst}
//| label: fig-pretraining-stages
//| fig-cap: "The same transaction fields under each stage. Pretraining reconstructs sampled amounts and merchants; fine-tuning makes them visible and hides every dispute label; prediction omits the labels."
//| fig-alt: "A grid with rows for amount, merchant, channel, and disputed and columns for pretraining, fine-tuning, and prediction. During pretraining a sampled amount position and a sampled merchant position are hidden and reconstructed, channel stays visible, and disputed is not in the schema. During fine-tuning amount, merchant, and channel are visible and disputed is hidden and supervised at every position. At prediction the inputs stay visible and disputed is predicted at every position."
#policies(
  ("Pretraining", "Fine-tuning", "Prediction"),
  (
    (label: [`amount` #linebreak() sampled reconstruction, then visible], cells: (("input", "input", "target", "input", "input"), repeat("input", 5), repeat("input", 5))),
    (label: [`merchant` #linebreak() sampled reconstruction, then visible], cells: (("input", "target", "input", "input", "input"), repeat("input", 5), repeat("input", 5))),
    (label: [`channel` #linebreak() visible throughout], cells: (repeat("input", 5), repeat("input", 5), repeat("input", 5))),
    (label: [`disputed` #linebreak() added at fine-tuning with `mask=True`], cells: (repeat("none", 5), repeat("target", 5), repeat("target", 5))),
  ),
)
```

Pretraining is optional. A supervised model can also start from newly
initialized weights. An ordinary float mask, such as `mask=0.15`, only supplies
input dropout; pretraining needs `reconstruct=True` to create an objective.

Reconstruction recovers amounts and merchants already present in the saved
sequence. The supervised labels keep their definitions from
[Profile context and a second outcome](profile-context-and-a-second-outcome.qmd): one
cutoff per observation and a 30-day window after it.

Once the model has learned from your histories, you can adapt it with labeled
examples or keep it fixed and test exported
[embeddings](reusable-representations.qmd) as inputs to separate task
predictors. Evaluate both choices against the existing task workflow on the
same held-out observations. The
[event-history guide](profile-context-and-a-second-outcome.qmd) explains how to define
observations, decision cutoffs, and future outcome windows.

## Pretrain on histories

Each pretraining row keeps `account_age_days` at the root and the booking
time, amount, merchant, and channel inside each transaction. The last booking
defines the snapshot cutoff; nothing after it enters the row. Observed
amounts and merchants provide their own supervision when selected values are
hidden, so no dispute or merchant-repeat label is needed:

```yaml
account_age_days: 420
trxns:
  - booked_at: "2026-03-28T09:00:00"
    amount: 24.00
    merchant: Harbor Internet
    channel: direct_debit
  - booked_at: "2026-04-28T09:00:00"
    amount: 24.00
    merchant: Harbor Internet
    channel: direct_debit
  - booked_at: "2026-05-27T08:00:00"
    amount: 32.00
    merchant: Station Cafe
    channel: card
  - booked_at: "2026-05-28T09:00:00"
    amount: 24.00
    merchant: Harbor Internet
    channel: direct_debit
```

Configure sampled reconstruction on `amount` and `merchant`, then fit using
separate application-supplied training and validation files in this shape:

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.xs(
    account_age_days=rf.Number,
    trxns=rf.Branch(
        length=32,
        overflow="tail",
        booked_at=rf.DateParts(
            dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"],
        ),
        amount=rf.Number(mask=rf.Mask(rate=0.15, reconstruct=True)),
        merchant=rf.Category(
            mask=rf.Mask(rate=0.15, reconstruct=True),
        ),
        channel=rf.Enum(values=("card", "direct_debit", "bank_transfer")),
    ),
)
pretraining_data = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    train="payments/pretraining/train.parquet",
    validate="payments/pretraining/validation.parquet",
)
model.fit(
    pretraining_data,
    batch_size=128,
    max_epochs=50,
    checkpoint_dir="checkpoints/payment-pretraining",
)
model.save("artifacts/payment-pretrained.rf")
```

The two paths identify independent, application-supplied Parquet files with
this richer record structure. Histories are sorted oldest to newest for
`overflow="tail"`. The profile, booking calendar, and channels remain visible
while selected transaction amounts and merchants are hidden. Keep preparation
consistent through the [preprocessing pipeline](../guides/preprocessing.qmd).

Each sampled value is predicted from the remaining context; unselected values
remain inputs. These fractional reconstruction policies also sample during
validation and test, but are inactive during ordinary prediction. See
[Masking and reconstruction](../concepts/masking-and-reconstruction.qmd) for selection and stage rules.

Fitting restores the best validation checkpoint before the artifact is saved.
See [Training options](../guides/training-options.qmd) for checkpoint selection.

## Adapt to a labeled task

For this adaptation, add a settled Boolean `disputed` label to every
transaction. Each answers the common-cutoff question above. All labeled
transaction positions contribute to the supervised objective.

Pretraining and fine-tuning splits must respect the same evaluation boundaries;
pretraining on held-out accounts or future observations changes what the
downstream evaluation measures.

Load the pretrained artifact, remove its sampled reconstruction policies, and
add a supervised label:

`rf.where("address")` selects nodes by their path in the declared model tree.
The first selector below chooses the amount and merchant fields for `update`;
the second chooses `trxns` as the parent for `extend` to add the new target.

```python
finetuned = rf.Model.load("artifacts/payment-pretrained.rf")
reconstructed_inputs = rf.where("address").is_in(
    [
        rf.Address("trxns", "amount"),
        rf.Address("trxns", "merchant"),
    ]
)
finetuned.update(reconstructed_inputs, mask=False)
finetuned.extend(
    rf.where("address") == rf.Address("trxns"),
    disputed=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
)
```

Amount and merchant remain visible inputs. `mask=True` keeps every dispute
label out of the input and uses it as supervision. If the target already
exists, update its mask to `True` instead of adding it again.

The profile, booking dates, and channel fields stay in place. To adapt to the
merchant-repeat outcome instead, add `repeats_next_30_days=rf.Boolean(mask=True)`
to `trxns` and supply every transaction's label for the same future window.
The [event-history guide](profile-context-and-a-second-outcome.qmd) shows both supervised
outcomes together.

```{typst}
//| label: fig-pretraining-transfer
//| fig-alt: "Account context contains account age and a trxns branch. Each transaction has booking date, amount, merchant, and channel. Pretraining reconstructs sampled amounts and merchants; fine-tuning predicts disputed for every transaction."
//| fig-cap: "The same transaction sequence supplies reconstruction context and each transaction's dispute prediction."
#tree(node("account", kind: "root", children: (
  node("account_age_days", width: 150pt, type: "Number"),
  node("trxns", kind: "branch", repeated: true, children: (
    node("booked_at", type: "DateParts"),

    node("channel", type: "Enum"),
    node("disputed", kind: "target", type: "Boolean", detail: "Each transaction"),

)))
```

Evolving the trained schema rebuilds modules and retains state entries whose
names, types, and tensor shapes still match. The new target starts with newly
initialized state; changing widths, field types, or structure can also reinitialize incompatible
parts. Keep existing addresses and geometry stable when reusing a pretrained
model. Adding a field can change context and reduction behavior even when
existing weights transfer. [Schema mutation](../guides/schema-mutation.qmd) describes
these boundaries.

## Start a new training run

Start a new fit with labeled Parquet files supplied by your application.
The call binds a fresh optimizer to the edited model, including its new target.
A smaller learning rate is a starting point to evaluate:

```python
finetuning_data = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    train="payments/finetuning/train.parquet",
    validate="payments/finetuning/validation.parquet",
)
finetuned.fit(
    finetuning_data,
    batch_size=128,
    learning_rate=1e-4,
    weight_decay=0.01,
    max_epochs=20,
    checkpoint_dir="checkpoints/payment-finetuning",
)
finetuned.save("artifacts/payment-disputes.rf")
```

This starts new optimization from the transferred model state. Use `ckpt_path`
with a full Lightning checkpoint when [resuming the same task](../guides/checkpoints-ema-and-resuming.qmd#resume-training),
including its optimizer and loop progress.
Reapply processors and desired compilation after loading and schema edits.
Pass any scheduler to this fit call; it is not inherited from pretraining.
For DDP, every rank must construct the same final schema.

Fine-tuning here updates the model end to end, including the new decoder and
existing encoders. Loaded [vocabularies](../concepts/online-vocabulary.qmd) and
Number normalization statistics also
continue learning from training observations; loading does not freeze them.
Validation, test, and prediction reuse that state. For a fixed feature extractor,
continue with [embeddings](reusable-representations.qmd): add `embed=True`
to this saved model's root or `trxns` branch, export in prediction mode, and
fit a separate predictor without updating the exporting model. This lets you
test the learned context for another outcome before choosing to fine-tune it.

At inference, omit `disputed` from every transaction and keep the transaction
records. The schema address is `/trxns/disputed`; prediction output
returns each retained transaction's result inside `predictions.trxns`, with
`inferred: true` at every position. See [Prediction output](../reference/prediction-output.qmd).

## Keep auxiliary objectives deliberately

To retain amount reconstruction alongside dispute, keep that policy when
adapting the pretrained artifact. Replace the earlier
`finetuned.update(reconstructed_inputs, mask=False)` call with:

```python
finetuned.update(
    rf.where("address") == rf.Address("trxns", "merchant"),
    mask=False,
)
finetuned.update(
    rf.where("address") == rf.Address("trxns", "amount"),
    weight=0.1,
)
```

Then add the dispute target and start the new run as above. Keeping the amount
policy preserves its trained decoder; removing reconstruction and later
reenabling it creates a new decoder. Both amount and dispute losses are now
optimized. `weight` scales the amount loss rather than its sampling rate or a
fixed fraction of the combined loss.

Compare fine-tuning against the same supervised task trained from scratch.
Use the same held-out data and dispute metric: pretraining loss and fine-tuning
loss have different objective sets and are not directly comparable. Retaining
auxiliary objectives may help or hurt the task, so evaluate that choice rather
than assuming pretraining guarantees a better model. See [Evaluation](evaluation.qmd).

## Evaluate vocabulary coverage

For large-vocabulary reconstruction, report how many selected answers the
model can express as well as how well it predicts them. For example, monitor
`.trxns.merchant/validate.coverage.content` alongside
`.trxns.merchant/validate.nll.content` and
`.trxns.merchant/validate.accuracy.all`.
The [Category metrics](../datatypes/category.qmd#vocabulary-and-learning) and
[Cluster metrics](../datatypes/cluster.qmd#learning-and-inspection)
define these denominators and count unavailable targets explicitly.

An unknown Category or Cluster target contributes no label gradient. Forcing its
prediction to be uniform over known labels would teach a different task, not
recover the missing answer. With no known targets, conditional reconstruction
quality is `NaN`; zero coverage means the validation objective is unmeasurable,
not that the model reconstructed everything perfectly. Cluster balancing and
adaptive-cluster updates also exclude unknown answers. Do not select a
checkpoint from such a conditional score without checking coverage.

Vocabulary growth can change the evaluated known-target population between
epochs. NLL can increase when newly admitted, difficult labels join it even
if predictions on the old labels improve. The summed validation loss is not a
coverage-adjusted model-quality score. Keep a fixed validation source, monitor
coverage, and compare known-target quality at comparable coverage. If necessary,
retain a fixed cohort of training-established labels for an additional stable
diagnostic; do not populate the model vocabulary from validation or test data.

Random reconstruction masks introduce another source of variation. For a
repeatable diagnostic, supply application-owned Boolean selection fields and
use `Mask(query=..., reconstruct=True)`. This fixes selected coordinates;
it does not freeze vocabulary growth or make unknown answers learnable.
Keep any held-out calibration set separate from model selection, and evaluate
downstream confidence separately for familiar and unseen input identities.

[P062](../evidence/vocabulary/pretraining-coverage.py) isolates vocabulary
coverage with fixed query-selected masks and checks that rebatching the same
targets cannot change the reported counts or conditional scores.
[P065](../evidence/vocabulary/cluster-pretraining-coverage.py) tests Cluster coverage.

[P066](../evidence/vocabulary/rolling-input-admission.py) separately checks cold
Category inputs across successive training cohorts. Its selected run records
zero admission drift and unchanged reconstruction NLL before an optimizer
step. One cold-cohort prediction-quality check remains unmet, so the overall
result remains unmet. Target coverage does not measure input familiarity:
keep input cohorts separate when assessing pretraining quality. These are
the selected run's measurements and retain its recorded library revision;
they are not a new execution against the current source.

[Set metrics](../datatypes/set.qmd#vocabulary-and-learning) count positive
memberships rather than scalar targets. A partial-OOV Set retains its known
positive and negative supervision; dropping the whole set would discard valid
evidence. An all-OOV set still supplies known negatives when annotations are
complete. Report member coverage, complete-set coverage, exact-set accuracy,
and micro F1 together. Empty sets are valued, complete annotations, although
an all-empty evaluation has no positive-member denominator. These semantics
are not appropriate for incompletely annotated labels without further masking.

Next, [reuse the learned context](reusable-representations.qmd) as input
to separate predictors, with the exporting model kept fixed.
